reference.source: Williams Obstetrics / RCOG and international fetal medicine guidance
clinicalPearls: TTTS is a complication of monochorionic twin pregnancies caused by unbalanced blood flow across shared placental vascular anastomoses
The donor twin becomes hypovolaemic, oliguric, and growth-restricted with oligohydramnios, appearing 'stuck' against the uterine wall
The recipient twin becomes hypervolaemic and polyuric with polyhydramnios and may develop cardiac overload and hydrops
Determining chorionicity in the first trimester is essential, as only monochorionic pregnancies are at risk
Diagnosis relies on the combination of oligohydramnios in one sac and polyhydramnios in the other on ultrasound
The Quintero system stages severity from amniotic fluid discordance through absent bladder filling, abnormal Dopplers, hydrops, to demise
Fetoscopic laser photocoagulation of the connecting placental anastomoses is the preferred treatment for significant disease
Amnioreduction and, in selected cases, selective reduction are alternative or adjunctive options depending on stage and gestation
reference.pathophysiology: In monochorionic twins a single shared placenta contains vascular anastomoses connecting the two foetal circulations. When net flow through unbalanced arteriovenous connections favours one twin, blood is chronically shunted from a donor to a recipient. The donor responds to relative hypovolaemia with reduced urine output and oligohydramnios and becomes growth-restricted, while the recipient develops volume overload, polyuria, and polyhydramnios, with activation of vasoactive and natriuretic pathways that can lead to cardiac hypertrophy, dysfunction, and hydrops. Without treatment the haemodynamic imbalance progresses and threatens both twins.
additionalDifferentials: Selective foetal growth restriction in monochorionic twins
Structural or chromosomal anomaly in one twin
additionalInvestigations: Serial ultrasound assessment of amniotic fluid volumes in each sac
Doppler studies of umbilical artery, middle cerebral artery, and ductus venosus
Foetal echocardiography, particularly of the recipient twin
Assessment of bladder filling and growth in each twin
Confirmation of chorionicity from early pregnancy imaging
Foetal anatomy survey to exclude coexisting anomalies
redFlags: Rapidly worsening polyhydramnios causing maternal discomfort or threatened preterm labour
Abnormal Doppler waveforms or absent bladder filling indicating advancing stage
Signs of foetal hydrops in the recipient
Sudden demise of one twin threatening the co-twin
reference.prognosis: Untreated advanced TTTS carries a high risk of loss of one or both twins. Fetoscopic laser therapy substantially improves survival and reduces neurological morbidity, though outcomes depend on stage at treatment and gestational age, and long-term neurodevelopmental follow-up is advised.
pitfalls: Failing to establish chorionicity early and missing the at-risk monochorionic pregnancy
Attributing amniotic fluid discordance to growth restriction alone and delaying referral
Not referring promptly to a fetal medicine centre capable of laser therapy
Overlooking the co-twin's risk after single intrauterine death
references: RCOG guidance on monochorionic twin pregnancy
International fetal medicine consensus on twin-to-twin transfusion syndrome
